stops: Welcome to the Han River in Da Nang. Ahead is the Dragon Bridge, six hundred and sixty-six metres long, linking downtown Hai Chau on the west bank with Son Tra district and My Khe Beach on the east bank.
Our first stop is the dragon's tail: a curling tail with flared fins at the west end of the bridge, facing the city centre.

Now we fly right over the deck. There are six traffic lanes, three in each direction, a six-metre central median, and two-and-a-half-metre sidewalks on both sides. In total, the bridge is thirty-seven and a half metres wide.
This is the two-hundred-metre main arch span, where the dragon's body rises highest. Steel hangers tie its belly to the deck.
From the water, you can see the five main spans resting on piers in the riverbed, with tour boats passing beneath the bridge.
This is the dragon's head, facing the sea. At nine p.m. on Saturday and Sunday nights, the dragon breathes fire, then sprays water.

In the distance stands the Tran Thi Ly Bridge, a seven-hundred-and-thirty-one-metre cable-stayed bridge with a single pylon, one hundred and forty-five metres tall, leaning twelve degrees. Its three cable planes form a sail filled with wind.
We finish with a view from the river mouth. Son Tra Mountain lies to the northeast, and the Hai Van range to the northwest.
ttlStops: The Tran Thi Ly Bridge is seven hundred and thirty-one metres long, with a single pylon leaning west like a sail filled with wind over the Han River.

This concrete pylon leans twelve degrees. It is one hundred and forty-five metres tall, rising one hundred and thirty-four metres above the deck, and it leans away from the two-hundred-and-thirty-metre main span to balance the pull of the cables.
Instead of being fixed to the pier, the pylon stands on two giant steel bearings, each carrying about two hundred and fifty thousand kilonewtons.
From the east bank at night, LEDs on the pylon, cables and deck shift through red, pink, purple and blue.

This is the front cable plane. A single semi-fan plane on the centreline anchors in the five-and-a-half-metre median of the main span. The deck is thirty-four and a half metres wide and carries six lanes.
In the two rear cable planes, the highest cable anchors nearest the pylon and the lowest farthest away, forming a hyperbolic surface when seen from below.
Just to the north is the old Nguyen Van Troi Bridge, a steel truss bridge that is now for pedestrians only.
tpStops: Thuan Phuoc Bridge is the last crossing on the Han River before it flows into Da Nang Bay. It is about one thousand eight hundred and fifty-six metres long.
We are under the four-hundred-and-five-metre main span. The aerodynamic steel box girder is welded from sixty-nine segments, and twenty-seven metres of clearance lets ships into the bay.
Two H-shaped reinforced-concrete towers rise eighty metres above their bases, with crossbeams at the top and beneath the deck.
At the top of the towers, the two main cables, three hundred and sixty millimetres across, pass over saddles. An aviation light blinks on each tower.
From the western approach, twelve fifty-metre prestressed-concrete spans on each side slope down to Nguyen Tat Thanh Street and the Son Tra peninsula.
Looking east is the Son Tra peninsula. One hundred and fourteen hangers, about nine point nine metres apart, tie the main cables to the girder.
At night, LEDs on the cables, hangers and towers shift through blue, purple, pink and green, flowing along the bridge like wind heading out to sea.
shStops: Opened on the twenty-ninth of March, two thousand, the Han River Bridge is Vietnam's only swing bridge. It is four hundred and eighty-seven point seven metres long and links Le Duan Street with Pham Van Dong Street.
We are above the turntable. The one-hundred-and-twenty-two-point-seven-metre centre span rotates ninety degrees around a round pier. On this tour, the bridge swings once at thirty times normal speed.
This is the turntable. The swing span rests on a rail ring and rollers around the pier, and a king pin keeps it centred as it turns.
From the Bach Dang riverside: when the bridge is open, the span lies along the river, leaving two channels for ships on either side of the pier.
On the deck, before swinging, the signals turn red and barriers drop at both ends of the span. Vehicles already on it drive off.
This ship's mast is about eleven metres taller than the bridge's clearance, so it can only pass when the bridge is open. In real life, the bridge swings at eleven p.m. on Saturday and Sunday nights.
